item.title: Part 2: Teaching RAG to Plan, Compare and Remember
item.dc:creator: Kanav Sharma
item.description:
Last weekPhase 0 The previous pipeline answered when Ashoka became a Buddhist. Six books, one paragraph, no sentence tied to a page.

The next question is shorter, and it is the one that breaks Phase 0.

How did he rule?

“He” is not a retrieval query. BM25 searches for the word. FAISS embeds a pronoun. Whatever comes back, the model fills in a king from pretraining, often the right one, for the wrong reason. Part 1 was the hybrid baseline. This post is Phase 1: the follow-up is rewritten before anything is searched, and two historians are held in separate lanes so they cannot be averaged.

This post is about how did I solved it: Phase 0 retrieves once, answers once, and forgets everything.

To solve it in Phase 1 I made the pipeline agentic. The full code is in the repo under phase_1_agentic_rag.

What Phase 0 does with a follow-up

Phase 0 has no memory. Every question is the first question. “How did he rule his subjects?” is embedded as-is, mixed with whatever chunks sit near the word “he”, and written up as one voice. The chunk ids come afterwards, in a pile, which is what I showed last week.

A conversation with a book is mostly follow-ups. I keep a scripted one in the Phase 1 entrypoint, because a single polished query never shows this bug.

  1. What did Guru Gobind Singh bring to Sikhi that was not there before?
  2. How did he shape it according to the political conditions?
  3. The militarisation of Sikhi, and his devotion to Shakti.
  4. How did he meet Banda Singh Bahadur, and what did Banda do after his death?
  5. Which battles did Banda fight, and how was he captured and killed?
  6. The same capture, asked again, shorter.
  7. What was his son’s name? Where was he from originally?
  8. Then a hard cut. When did Ashoka become a Buddhist, before or after Kalinga, and why?
  9. How did he take on the empire of his grandfather, and what did he add?
  10. What did Ahilyabai Holkar actually do?
  11. Which temples did she restore, and how, Somnath and Kashi?

Turns 2 to 7 are the same thread. “He” has to become Gobind Singh, and then, once Banda is the subject, Banda. Turn 7 is worse than a pronoun. Whose son? Turn 8 is a different century. If memory is doing its job, Ashoka is not answered out of the Sikh turns. Turn 9 is “he” again, and now “he” has to be Ashoka, not Banda. Turn 11 is “she”.

I am not pasting model answers for that conversation. A fluent paragraph hides the only line that matters. On each turn I print the rewritten question. If turn 9 still says Banda, the agent failed, whatever the prose looks like.

What Phase 1 does before it retrieves

Two models. A small one, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, does the rewrite and the plan. The same 4-bit model as Phase 0 writes the answer. Planning is cheap and allowed to be wrong. The answer is the thing I do not want improvised.

Memory goes first. A question is a follow-up if it contains a pronoun, or if its embedding is close to the previous question, cosine above 0.55. The pronoun list is blunt: he, she, they, his, her, him, it, this, that, and a few cousins. If it is not a follow-up, I wipe the history. A new topic should not inherit the previous century. If it is a follow-up, I keep the last turns and append this question with an empty answer, which the synthesizer fills in later.

The rewrite uses that history and nothing else. The small model sees the last three turns. In the prompt, each previous answer is clipped to 200 characters. The instruction is narrow. If the question says he, she, they, it, or this, replace it with the person from the history. If the question already stands on its own, return it unchanged. Output only the question. If the result is shorter than a few characters, I throw it away and keep the original. I would rather search a pronoun than search a garbled sentence.

The planner turns one question into lanes. It has to return JSON: up to four historians, a sub-question for the work, whether a comparison was asked for, and one sentence on why. I parse it. If it is not JSON, the plan becomes a single lane called general and the rewritten question. The agent falls back toward Phase 0. It does not crash into a half-written plan.

Your names beat the planner. If you pass --historians, those labels are the lanes, and the model’s guess is ignored. That was deliberate. I do not want a 1.5B model deciding that “the nationalist view” is a person.

Lanes are zipped, one historian with one sub-question. If the planner wrote one sub-question and I asked for two historians, that question is copied into both lanes. The historians differ. The question does not. If the two lists disagree in length, both lanes get the rewritten question rather than a mismatched pair I cannot explain.

Retrieval inside a lane is not the full Phase 0 stack, and I should say so.

If I can resolve the name to a per-historian FAISS index on disk, that lane searches only there. Names are normalised, then fuzzy-matched, SequenceMatcher at 0.75, so “RK Mukherjee” can still land on the Mukherjee bucket. I take that dense search and keep seven passages. There is no BM25 in that path, and no cross-encoder. I gave up the lexical channel on purpose. A nearer sentence from someone else must not be able to outrank Thapar inside Thapar’s lane.

If the folder is missing, the lane falls back to the Phase 0 hybrid retriever, BM25 plus FAISS plus the reranker, and I tag the metadata with the historian I asked for. The tag is not a wall. On a fresh clone, where index/ is gitignored and the per-historian folders were never built, both lanes search the same global pile. The header will still say Thapar. The passages might not.

The lanes run in parallel. Each one writes its own key into retrieved_results, and a dict merge keeps them from clobbering each other. Then a position object is built per lane: historian, passages, chunk ids.

What the synthesizer is allowed to see

The evidence is not one bag. It is blocked.

--- LANE_0 ---
Historian: Romila Thapar

[chunk_id=EARLY_INDIA_RTH_...] first 300 characters of the passage

--- LANE_1 ---
Historian: R.K. Mukherjee

[chunk_id=ASOKA_RKM_...] first 300 characters of the passage

The outline above that evidence is a keyword switch, not a classifier. “Why” and “how did” get causes, evidence, interpretation. “Who” gets the person. “Compare” gets a comparison. Anything else gets a default of context, developments, evidence, significance. I would rather a slightly wrong heading than a model inventing its own structure and wandering off the pages.

The instruction is stricter than Phase 0, and also less honest about it. Phase 0 forbade the model from writing chunk ids, and I appended them myself. Phase 1 tells the model that every claim must cite [chunk_id=...], and then I still append up to twenty unique ids at the bottom. I do not trust the inline cites yet. The dump is the part I can check. The inline cite is the part I am trying to grow up into, which is Part 5, not this one.

Memory is updated from the answer, not from the whole answer. I store 400 characters. Past five turns, the older ones are summarised by the small model into a single note, and the recent five stay verbatim. The summary keeps names. It does not keep pages. That is good enough to resolve “she” to Ahilyabai. It is not good enough to cite her.

The command I actually want you to run:

python -m phase_1_agentic_rag.run_query \
  --query "How did Ashoka rule his subjects?" \
  --historians "Romila Thapar,R.K. Mukherjee" \
  --answer_style concise

Interactive, so you can ask “how did he rule?” as the second turn:

python -m phase_1_agentic_rag.run_query --interactive

There is a Gradio UI on --gradio. Same graph. The README in the Phase 1 folder still mentions an old module name, phase_1_newtesting. The command above is the one that exists.

The number I do not have

Phase 0 at least had a ROUGE, and I told you not to trust it. Phase 1’s --evaluate flag does not score anything. It runs that eleven-turn conversation and prints, for each turn, the rewritten question and the answer.

That is the right smoke test and a bad evaluation. I can see whether “he” survived. I cannot tell you whether Thapar’s lane stayed inside Thapar, or whether a cited chunk id actually contains the sentence. I am not going to invent a faithfulness number for a system I have not measured that way. The trace is the result. If the rewritten line is wrong, nothing downstream is worth reading.

What I am not claiming

A lane is a wall between authors. It is not a historian, and it is not a graph.

“His son” is not clarified. It is guessed. The rewriter must return a question, not a question back. After a turn that mentions both Gobind Singh and Banda, “what was his son’s name?” will be resolved to somebody. A research assistant would ask which he. Mine picks. The pronoun list makes this worse in the other direction too. “This” and “that” count as follow-ups, so a fresh question that merely contains “that” inherits the previous person. And a real follow-up with no pronoun and different wording can fall under 0.55 and get its history wiped. Both errors are mine. The threshold is a constant I have not earned.

The comparison node is not doing the comparison. There is a claim aligner. It runs only if the planner sets use_claim_aligner. When it runs, it looks for structured claims on the lane. The position extractor never writes those claims. It writes passages. So the disagreement JSON is usually empty, and the thing that actually keeps the historians apart is the lane header in the prompt. I would rather show you that than pretend a node named “aligner” is reconciling Majumdar with Thapar.

Two passages count as enough. The evaluator replans if it sees fewer than two passages, and it will only do that once. Then it declares the evidence sufficient and synthesizes. Two chunks is a guard against an empty index. It is not a reading of the pages. Calling it an evaluator in a diagram is already more credit than the if statement deserves.

The model does not see the page. Each passage is clipped to 300 characters before synthesis. A qualification, a date, a “but his son”, often lives past character 300. Hybrid search can retrieve the right chunk and the prompt can still cut off the sentence that mattered. I have not fixed the clip.

A named lane drops BM25. Inside a historian index I search dense-only. Ashoka and Asoka are the sort of variation I built BM25 for in Phase 0, and the lane gives that up. The fallback, when the index folder is absent, gives up the wall instead. I do not currently have both.

None of this answers “did Savarkar’s writing reach Bhagat Singh?” A lane can hand me Thapar’s passages and Mukherjee’s passages. It still needs one chunk that happens to contain both people, or the model will build the edge itself. That edge is Part 3. People, organisations, a timeline, checked against the vector hits rather than hoped for inside a 1,600-character window.

Code: github.com/mekanavsharma/the-digital-historian

Next Saturday

Part 3 is the same books, and a question a lane cannot represent. Who was associated with Abhinav Bharat, and which of those links is actually written down?

I want the relation to come from a graph I can open, not from a paragraph that sounds like it read one. If the graph and the pages disagree, the pages win. That rule is the whole post.

item.title: Part 1: Why vanilla RAG isn’t enough for historical research
item.dc:creator: Kanav Sharma
item.description:
I have spent my career building models on numbers: tabular data, time series, forecasting. Over the last couple of years my work moved to LLMs, RAG and agents. At work I could use RAG on business data. But I wanted to understand it properly, end to end, on a problem where I could feel when the answer was wrong.

So I picked a topic I love: Indian history.

This post is the first in a series on The Digital Historian , a multi-phase RAG project I am building. I am learning as I go, so I will share the mistakes along with the wins. In this part I want to answer one question:

If RAG exists, why can’t I just plug my history books into a vanilla RAG pipeline and call it done?

What I mean by “vanilla RAG”

Almost every RAG tutorial follows the same four steps:

  1. Split documents into chunks.
  2. Convert each chunk into an embedding and store it in a vector database.
  3. At question time, embed the question and fetch the top-k most similar chunks.
  4. Paste those chunks into a prompt and let the LLM write the answer.

For a company FAQ or product manual, this works surprisingly well. I got a first version running in a day. Then I started asking it real history questions, and it fell apart in ways that were hard to notice, because the answers sounded confident.

Why history is a hard domain for RAG

My corpus is a set of Indian history books, converted to text with OCR. Working with it showed me few problems that tutorials never mention.

The text is OCR, not prose. One volume of The History and Culture of the Indian People took about 22 minutes to extract. Scans are not consistent. André Wink’s Al-Hind, Volume 2, is two book pages on one image. Chapter titles and stray page numbers leak into the body. A hyphen at the end of a line becomes a word the embedder has never seen. If you embed that as if it were a clean Wikipedia paragraph, you are embedding the scanner.

Dates, names and spellings confuse embeddings The same king shows up as Ashoka, Asoka, and the Mauryan emperor who issued the Kalinga edicts. A dense embedding often places those near each other. It does not have to. BM25 will not miss the spelling that is actually on the page. Dense search will not miss the description when the name is missing. Use only one of them and you will systematically drop one kind of evidence. Same goes for Battle of Panipat we had 3 battles 1526, 1556 and 1761.To an embedding model, “Battle of Panipat” chunks all look alike. Ask about the 1556 battle and you can easily get Babur’s 1526 victory or the Maratha defeat in 1761.

The question is often a constraint, not a topic. “Before or after Kalinga” is a relation in time. Cosine similarity retrieves passages about Ashoka and passages about Kalinga. It does not retrieve the relation. The model then fills the relation in from pretraining, which is the textbook story I was trying not to trust.

The sources disagree on purpose. While I was cleaning the data I labelled every chunk with a period (Ancient, Medieval, Modern) and a perspective (Nationalist, Marxist, Neutral). Phase 0 stores those labels. At query time it ignores them. The nearest chunk wins, the model blends, and a disagreement becomes a smooth paragraph. An average of historians is not a citation.

What Phase 0 actually does

I did not ship that pipeline. I shipped the smallest system I was willing to measure. Fully local. No external API.

A chunk at rank r scores weight / (r + k). If BM25 and FAISS both return the same chunk_id, I keep the document once and add the scores. The cross-encoder then reads the question next to the passage and reorders that list. Only ten chunks are allowed into the prompt, and the prompt is capped at about 10,000 characters.

The instruction to the model is not polite. Use only the context. Do not bring in outside knowledge. If the context has nothing, say you don’t know. Write a paragraph. Do not invent chunk_id tokens. I append those myself, after generation, from the chunks that were actually in the prompt. I do not trust the model to cite.

Length is a parameter, not a vibe: short, concise, or detailed, with an optional word cap.

The part that took the time was not the retriever. It was the pages.

After OCR I strip chapter headers, standalone page numbers, and hyphenation across line breaks. I do not cut a page in isolation. A slice of the previous page and the next page is carried onto the current page, so a claim that crosses a page break still exists, and the page number stays attached. A recursive splitter then cuts that into chunks of about 1,600 characters with 200 characters of overlap. Every chunk gets an id that I can read without opening the file:

HCIP_RCM_V2_C5_P143_1

series, volume, chapter, page, piece. Building the FAISS index over the full corpus took about 50 minutes on a Kaggle P100. After that the index is just read. The processed corpus is 167 MB of JSONL, on Kaggle, because it does not belong in git.

One answer, seven chunk ids

This is a real run, concise style.

Query: Can you check and tell when did Ashoka became Buddhist was it before or after Kalinga, why did he became?

Ashoka became Buddhist before the Kalinga war. According to the context, he became a Buddhist before the Kalinga war, around 265 BCE, as an upasaka. The remorse he felt after the Kalinga war deepened his belief in Buddhism, leading him to adopt it as a central pursuit. This conversion was not immediate but developed gradually over time, culminating in a strong commitment to Buddhist principles and practices. The Kalinga war served as a catalyst for his spiritual transformation, prompting him to seek solace and guidance in Buddhism.

[chunk_id=HCIP_RCM_V2_C5_P143_1]
[chunk_id=ASOKA_RKM_C2_P43_1]
[chunk_id=EARLY_INDIA_RTH_C6_P288_0]
[chunk_id=GEM_LOTUS_AE_C6_P486_1]
[chunk_id=AL_HIND_AW_V2_C10_P176_2]
[chunk_id=EARLY_INDIA_RTH_C6_P262_1]
[chunk_id=WTWI_ALB_C3_P112_1]

The content is more careful than the textbook line. It says he was an upasaka before the war, around 265 BCE, and that Kalinga deepened a belief that was already there. I am not asking you to treat that as settled. I am asking you to look at how it is written.

“According to the context” is not a historian’s phrase. It is the prompt leaking into the answer. And then the last line:

Prefix Where it came from
HCIP_RCM The History and Culture of the Indian People, R.C. Majumdar
ASOKA_RKM Asoka, R.K. Mukherjee
EARLY_INDIA_RTH Early India, Romila Thapar
GEM_LOTUS_AE Gem in the Lotus, Abraham Eraly
AL_HIND_AW Al-Hind, André Wink
WTWI_ALB The Wonder That Was India, A.L. Basham

Seven ids. Six books. One paragraph. No sentence is tied to a book. If Thapar and Majumdar diverge inside those pages, this format cannot say so. It can only look sure.

That is the hole. Hybrid search got me into the right neighbourhood. It did not give me a historian.

The number I do not want quoted back at me

On the evaluation set I had for this config, hybrid retrieval plus the reranker scored about ROUGE-1 0.44 and ROUGE-L 0.29 against the reference answers.

I am publishing it because a baseline without a number is a demo. I am also telling you not to be impressed.

ROUGE counts overlapping words. A fluent paragraph that picks the wrong side of a debate can beat a short, correct, cited one. It cannot see the failure I actually care about, which is attribution. It cannot tell “the context supports this” from “the model remembered this from pretraining and the context happened to rhyme.” Later in the series the measurement moves to faithfulness, context precision, and whether a citation points at the sentence that was used. ROUGE can stay as a sanity check. It is not the verdict.

There is a second honesty problem in the harness. It reports the hybrid system. It does not yet report BM25 alone, FAISS alone, and hybrid side by side. So I will not claim, in this post, that I have measured the gap. The argument above is about what a single ranked list cannot represent. The ablation is still owed.

Five breaks that a better top-k will not fix

These are from questions I actually run.

1. One voice. “How did Ashoka rule his subjects?” is not the same question in Thapar and in Mukherjee. Phase 0 retrieves both if they sit near the query, then writes a single answer. Comparison is a different task. It needs a lane per historian, and a step that refuses to merge them until someone asks for the comparison. That is Part 2.

2. The follow-up. “Why did he?” is not a retrieval query. Phase 0 has no memory. The pronoun goes into BM25 as the word “he”. The question has to be rewritten into “Why did Ashoka become a Buddhist?” before anything is searched. That is also Part 2.

3. A relation that no single chunk holds. “Did Savarkar’s writing reach Bhagat Singh?” is two people and an edge. Top-k returns essays about each of them. It returns the edge only when some 1,600-character window happens to contain both names. Part 3 puts people, organisations and a timeline in a graph, and checks that against the vector hits instead of hoping the chunk boundary was kind.

4. The right shelf, not the nearest chunk. A question about the drain of wealth, and a question about the same years written as a nationalist narrative, should not be answered from the same pile. The labels are already on the chunks. Phase 0 does not filter on them. Part 4 routes the question to a period and a perspective, keeps only those chunks, and fine-tunes the generator so it answers from the retrieved pages and ignores the distractors that retrieval always lets through.

5. A citation you can check. Appending every chunk id that entered the prompt is an honest description of what the model was shown. It is not a citation. A citation is: this sentence, that page. Part 5 trains that behaviour, then runs a generate, critique, refine loop that is allowed to rewrite only when a faithfulness score fails. The model’s own confidence is not the score.

Two smaller choices I am not promoting into their own phase. The reranker only sees the first 1,024 characters of a chunk. Generation samples at temperature 0.3. For a system whose job is to stay on the page, sampling is a luxury. I would rather be repetitive than inventive. I have not turned it off. I am writing it down so the knob stays a decision and not a default I forgot about.

What I am not claiming

Phase 0 is a control. It is local, it cites the chunks it saw, and it will say it doesn’t know when the prompt is doing its job. It is not a research assistant.

It will not tell you when two books conflict. It will not hold the thread of a conversation. It will not refuse a nearest-neighbour answer that came from the wrong school of history. A small model still walks past a strict prompt in boring ways, and ROUGE will clap for it.

If you want to run the control yourself:

python -m phase_0_rag_baseline.run_query \
  --query "When did Ashoka become a Buddhist, before or after Kalinga, and why?" \
  --answer_style concise

Code: github.com/mekanavsharma/the-digital-historian

Corpus: Indian History JSONL on Kaggle

Next Saturday

Part 2 is the same corpus and the same hybrid retriever. The difference is the thing I actually want to show. Not the framework. A follow-up, “how did he rule?”, rewritten to Ashoka before search runs, and two historians held in separate lanes so they cannot be averaged into a paragraph that neither of them wrote.

# actual path to train image folder
train_path = Path('/content/food-101/images')
test_path = Path('/content/food-101/test')

# Create Test folder

import os
import random
import shutil

def move_images_to_test(source_folder, test_folder, percentage=0.1):
    # Create the test folder if it doesn't exist
    os.makedirs(test_folder, exist_ok=True)

    # Iterate through each subfolder in the source folder
    for subfolder in os.listdir(source_folder):
        subfolder_path = os.path.join(source_folder, subfolder)

        # Check if it's a directory
        if os.path.isdir(subfolder_path):
            # Get a list of all image files in the subfolder
            image_files = [f for f in os.listdir(subfolder_path) if f.endswith('.jpg')]

            # Calculate the number of images to move
            num_images_to_move = int(len(image_files) * percentage)

            # Randomly select images to move
            images_to_move = random.sample(image_files, num_images_to_move)

            # Move selected images to the test folder
            for image in images_to_move:
                source_path = os.path.join(subfolder_path, image)
                dest_path = os.path.join(test_folder, image)
                shutil.move(source_path, dest_path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    move_images_to_test(train_path, test_path, percentage=0.15)

Dataloaders

Let’s create Dataloaders & to do that we will use DataBlock API, which is convenient in achieving our goal.

dls = DataBlock(
    blocks=(ImageBlock,CategoryBlock,CategoryBlock),
    n_inp=1,
    get_items=get_image_files,

Explanation of the code

blocks=(ImageBlock,CategoryBlock,CategoryBlock)

It will generate three outputs: an image (which we want to use for training), a categorical variable representing the calorie content, and another categorical variable representing the food type. We can add as many additional features as needed.

This line will tell our dataloader that only 1 of them(1st block i.e ImageBlock) is Independent variable & other two are target variable.

Use get_image_files to get a list of inputs.

To create the two outputs for each file, call two functions: parent_label (from fastai) and get_calorie (defined above).

Replicating the Food model

Now we’ll replicate the same food model we’ve made before, but have it work with this new data.

The key difference is that our metrics and loss will now receive three things instead of two: the model outputs (i.e. the metric and loss function inputs), and the two targets (food_type and calorie). Therefore, we need to define slight variations of our metric (error_rate) and loss function (cross_entropy) to pass on just the food_type target:

def food_err(inp,food,calorie): return error_rate(inp,food)
def food_loss(inp,food,calorie): return F.cross_entropy(inp,food)

We’re now ready to create our learner.

There’s just one wrinkle to be aware of. Now that our DataLoaders is returning multiple targets, fastai doesn’t know how many outputs our model will need. Therefore we have to pass n_out when we create our Learner – we need 101 outputs(no of food type), one for each possible disease:

We had a model that predicted 101 things(no of food types) and among these, whichever has the highest probability(food type) will assign ed to that image. Now, I want to have a model that can predict 202 things(101 food type + 101 calorie count).

We can define disease_loss just like we did earlier, but with one important change: the input tensor is now of length 202, not 101, so it doesn’t match the number of possible food type. We can pick whatever part of the input we want to be used to predict food type. Let’s use the first 101 values:

Under-sampling

Previously, we had very big data to be trained on, which is why it took so long to train our model. GPU Problem

In the previous file, we encountered a problem regarding GPU, where we run out of memory & have to wait to till our memory was cleared by Kaggle(on Saturday). We can use Gradient accumulation or Half-Precision floating point to save from future GPU constraints. Regarding Half-Precision floating point, we tested it in our first notebook of this series and observed minimal change in performance.

Gradient Accumulation

Working of Gradient Accumulation :

  • Forward pass: Input data is fed through the model to compute predictions.

  • Backward pass: Gradients are computed by back-propagating the error through the network.

  • Gradients are accumulated over multiple mini-batches.

  • Model parameters are updated after a certain number of mini-batches.

By accumulating gradients over multiple batches,it allows to simulate the effects of a larger batch size without exceeding the available memory.

However, there is a catch that it can have Impact on Training Time. While increasing accumulation can save GPU memory, it may also slow down the training process. The model parameters are updated less frequently, potentially prolonging the convergence time.

fine_tune() vs fit_one_cycle()

fine_tune() It uses transfer learning, where it take a pre-trained model (on ImageNet) & fine-tune it on a specific dataset. Idea is to leverage features learned by the pre-trained model & adapt them to new dataset.

It uses ‘discriminative learning rates’, where earlier layers are trained with lower learning rates (taking more time but understand data better) to avoid disrupting the general features they have learned. In contrast, later layers are trained with higher learning rates to adapt more quickly to the new tasks.

fit_one_cycle() It used for training a model from scratch or for further fine tuning already fine tuned model.

  • It starts with low learning rate & gradually increases it over the courses of first half of learning rate.

  • In second half it decreases.

  • This cyclical pattern of learning rates is repeated for no of epochs specified.

fine_tune() is primarily used for transfer learning, leveraging pre-trained models & adapting them to new data. While fit_one_cycle() is used for training models from scratch or further fine-tuning them using a cyclical learning rate schedule.

fine_tune() is faster since it doesn’t do an initial fine-tuning of the head.

def move_images_to_test(source_folder, test_folder, percentage=0.1):

    for subfolder in os.listdir(source_folder):

            image_files = [f for f in os.listdir(subfolder_path) if f.endswith('.jpg')]

Computer Vision Model(s) Understanding

In previous lecture , we referred to Which Image models are best? to understand computer vision models in general and which among them works best.

But this time, we will be deep diving into these models : Best Vision Model for fine-tuning. We have divided our testing in 2 parts :

  1. Existing Images : Our models, such as ConvNext and ResNet, have been trained on a set of 22,000 images from the ImageNet dataset. It is highly probable that our model has already been exposed to commonly encountered categories such as cats, cars, musical instruments, and more during its training.
  2. New Images : Here we are using Images that most probably are not in ImagNet dataset, like satellite images, medical images etc.

Our key findings :

  • In Case 1, both convnext_tiny_in22k and convnext_tiny emerged as go-to models, selected based on their impressive accuracy and efficient training times.

  • In Case 2, models like ViT (Vision Transformer) and Swin demonstrated excellent performance. Their transformer architecture proved beneficial in understanding patterns from the data they were not trained on previously, namely - vit_small_patch32_224, vit_small_patch16_224, swin_base_patch4_window7_224_in22k.

We don’t have test dataset, so let’s randomly create a test folder containing 15% of the images from train folder. Our model will not be trained on these images.

import os
import random
import shutil

def move_images_to_test(source_folder, test_folder, percentage=0.1):
    # Create the test folder if it doesn't exist
    os.makedirs(test_folder, exist_ok=True)

    # Iterate through each subfolder in the source folder
    for subfolder in os.listdir(source_folder):
        subfolder_path = os.path.join(source_folder, subfolder)

        # Check if it's a directory
        if os.path.isdir(subfolder_path):
            # Get a list of all image files in the subfolder
            image_files = [f for f in os.listdir(subfolder_path) if f.endswith('.jpg')]

            # Calculate the number of images to move
            num_images_to_move = int(len(image_files) * percentage)

            # Randomly select images to move
            images_to_move = random.sample(image_files, num_images_to_move)

            # Move selected images to the test folder
            for image in images_to_move:
                source_path = os.path.join(subfolder_path, image)
                dest_path = os.path.join(test_folder, image)
                shutil.move(source_path, dest_path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    train_path = Path('/content/food-101/images')

Focusing on Computer Vision and Tabular Data

My primary focus is to write on the lessons and techniques related to building and training models for Computer Vision tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and segmentation. Additionally, I’ll be exploring the methods and best practices for working with Tabular Data for this lecture only.

This chapter focuses on Tabular Data

from fastai.tabular.all import *
set_seed(42)

Read & Prepare the data

df = pd.read_csv('../input/titanic/train.csv')
df.head(10)

       'Major', 'Lady', 'Sir', 'Mlle', 'Col', 'Capt', 'the Countess',
       'Jonkheer'], dtype=object)
def add_features(df):
    df['LogFare'] = np.log1p(df['Fare'])
    df['Deck'] = df.Cabin.str[0].map(dict(A="ABC", B="ABC", C="ABC", D="DE", E="DE", F="FG", G="FG"))
    df['Family'] = df.SibSp+df.Parch
    df['Alone'] = df.Family==0
    df['TicketFreq'] = df.groupby('Ticket')['Ticket'].transform('count')
    df['Title'] = df.Name.str.split(', ', expand=True)[1].str.split('.', expand=True)[0]
    df['Title'] = df.Title.map(dict(Mr="Mr",Miss="Miss",Mrs="Mrs",Master="Master"))

add_features(df)
  • df[‘LogFare’] = np.log1p(df[‘Fare’]) It will create a column LogFare with Log() value of Fare column
  • df[‘Deck’] = df.Cabin.str[0].map(dict(A=“ABC”, B=“ABC”, C=“ABC”, D=“DE”, E=“DE”, F=“FG”, G=“FG”)) It will create a new ‘Deck’ column based on the first letter of the ‘Cabin’ column. The mapping is done to categorize cabins into groups (ABC, DE, FG).
  • df[‘Family’] = df.SibSp+df.Parch It will create a new column ‘Family’ which is the sum of the ‘SibSp’ (number of siblings/spouses) and ‘Parch’ (number of parents/children) columns.
  • df[‘Alone’] = df.Family == 0 It will create a column ‘Alone’ for those who don’t have family.
  • df[‘TicketFreq’] = df.groupby(‘Ticket’)[‘Ticket’].transform(‘count’) Adds a ‘TicketFreq’ column, representing the frequency of each ticket in the dataset.
  • df[‘Title’] = df.Name.str.split(‘,’, expand=True)[1].str.split(‘.’, expand=True)[0] Extracts the title from the ‘Name’ column (e.g., Mr, Miss, Mrs) and assigns it to a new ‘Title’ column.
  • df[‘Title’] = df.Title.map(dict(Mr=“Mr”,Miss=“Miss”,Mrs=“Mrs”,Master=“Master”)) Will take into account only these 3 titles anything else will be labelled as “NAN”.
#we can use RandomSplitter to separate out the training and validation sets:
    
splits = RandomSplitter(seed=42)(df)
dls = TabularPandas(
    df, splits=splits,
    procs = [Categorify, FillMissing, Normalize],
    cat_names=["Sex","Pclass","Embarked","Deck", "Title"],
    cont_names=['Age', 'SibSp', 'Parch', 'LogFare', 'Alone', 'TicketFreq', 'Family'],
    y_names="Survived", y_block = CategoryBlock(),
).dataloaders(path=".")
/opt/conda/lib/python3.10/site-packages/fastai/tabular/core.py:312: FutureWarning: A value is trying to be set on a copy of a DataFrame or Series through chained assignment using an inplace method.
The behavior will change in pandas 3.0. This inplace method will never work because the intermediate object on which we are setting values always behaves as a copy.

For example, when doing 'df[col].method(value, inplace=True)', try using 'df.method({col: value}, inplace=True)' or df[col] = df[col].method(value) instead, to perform the operation inplace on the original object.
  to[n].fillna(self.na_dict[n], inplace=True)

Tabular Pandas

  • splits=splits Use splits for indices of training and validation sets

  • procs = [Categorify, FillMissing, Normalize] Turn strings into categories, fill missing values in numeric columns with the median, normalise all numeric columns

  • cat_names will have all categorical columns

  • cont_names will have all continuous columns

  • y_names will have dependent variable

  • y_block() The dependent variable is categorical (so build a classification model, not a regression model) possible values RegressionBlock(), CategoryBlock(),MultiCategoryBlock()

Train the model

Call dataloader(dls) in tabular_learner & set size of hidden layer = [15,19] defualt is [200,100] layers parameter defines number of neurons in particular neural network.

Architecure of Shallow Neural network: 1. Input Layer 2. First Hidden Layer (15 in our case) 3. Second Hidden Layer (19 in our case) 4. Output Layer

Source

learn = tabular_learner(dls, metrics=accuracy, layers=[15,19])

Learning Rate

New Lr Finder Output

lr_min, lr_steep, lr_valley, lr_slide = learn.lr_find(suggest_funcs=(minimum, steep, valley, slide))

Lr_find(suggest_func= (slide, valley)) is great way to find learning rate for any model. There are multiple ways of do this, and in this case, we are using slide& valley methods. By picking one value among these two values we will get pretty good learning rate value

Generally it is established that: Valley > Slide > Steep > Minimum. Hence by defualt we use valley & slide to get best of both.

learn.lr_find(suggest_funcs=(slide, valley))
SuggestedLRs(slide=0.05754399299621582, valley=0.009120108559727669)

The two colored points are both reasonable choices for a learning rate. I’ll pick somewhere between the two (0.04) and train for a few epochs:

Submit to Kaggle

To submit to Kaggle, we’ll need to read in the test set, and do the same feature engineering we did for the training set:

tst_df = pd.read_csv('../input/titanic/test.csv')
tst_df['Fare'] = tst_df.Fare.fillna(0)
add_features(tst_df)

We don’t have to worry about pre-processing in our test dataset , we can call test_dl(), but we have to take care of NA value in target column if it didn’t existed in training because NA in target column wasn’t pre-processed so our function test_dl() do not have it’s recollection.

tst_dl = learn.dls.test_dl(tst_df)
/opt/conda/lib/python3.10/site-packages/fastai/tabular/core.py:312: FutureWarning: A value is trying to be set on a copy of a DataFrame or Series through chained assignment using an inplace method.
The behavior will change in pandas 3.0. This inplace method will never work because the intermediate object on which we are setting values always behaves as a copy.

For example, when doing 'df[col].method(value, inplace=True)', try using 'df.method({col: value}, inplace=True)' or df[col] = df[col].method(value) instead, to perform the operation inplace on the original object.

to[n].fillna(self.na_dict[n], inplace=True)

Now we can use get_preds to get the predictions for the test set:

preds,_ = learn.get_preds(dl=tst_dl)

Let’s get our predictions

tst_df['Survived'] = (preds[:,1]>0.6).int()
sub_df = tst_df[['PassengerId','Survived']]

Ensembling

We can create five separate models, each trained from different random starting points, and average them. This is the simplest approach of ensemble model

def ensemble():
    learn = tabular_learner(dls, metrics=accuracy, layers=[20,18])
    with learn.no_bar(),learn.no_logging(): learn.fit(12, lr=0.05)
    return learn.get_preds(dl=tst_dl)[0]

Now we run this five times, and collect the results into a list:

learns = [ensemble() for _ in range(5)]

We stack this predictions together and take their average predictions:

ens_preds = torch.stack(learns).mean(0)

Finally, use the same code as before to generate a submission file, which we can submit to Kaggle after the notebook is saved and run:

tst_df['Survived'] = (ens_preds[:,1]>0.55).int()

def get_data(part, col):
    df = pd.read_csv(f'benchmark-{part}-amp-nhwc-pt111-cu113-rtx3090.csv').merge(Benchmark_Result, on='model')
    df['secs'] = 1. / df[col]
    df['family'] = df.model.str.extract('^([a-z]+?(?:v2)?)(?:\d|_|$)')
    df = df[~df.model.str.endswith('gn')]
    df.loc[df.model.str.contains('in22'),'family'] = df.loc[df.model.str.contains('in22'),'family'] + '_in22'
    df.loc[df.model.str.contains('resnet.*d'),'family'] = df.loc[df.model.str.contains('resnet.*d'),'family'] + 'd'
    return df[df.family.str.contains('^re[sg]netd?|beit|convnext|levit|efficient|vit|vgg|swin')]

2. Prepare data for model training (Data Loaders, Data Augmentaion, etc.).

Create a data block and load that data block in data loader.

  • Data Block - Is a blueprint on how to assemble data that we want to send for training.
  • Data Loader - Is used to pass that data which is in batch format(i.e created using data blocks) to the GPU.
big_cat = DataBlock(
    blocks=(ImageBlock, CategoryBlock),
    get_items=get_image_files,
    splitter=RandomSplitter(valid_pct=0.2, seed=42),
    get_y=parent_label,
    item_tfms=Resize(128))
dls = big_cat.dataloaders(path)

DataBlock is a convenient way to organize the data loading, splitting, and transformation steps in preparation for training a deep learning model using the fastai library.

DataBlock(): is suitable for a classification task where you have a dataset of images, and each image belongs to a specific category (e.g., types of cats).

blocks=(ImageBlock, CategoryBlock): It specify that our inputs are images & our targets are categories(types of big cat)

get_image_files: This helps to get list of all the images from subfolder.

parent_label: This is a function that extracts the labels (categories) for each item.’Leapord’,‘Tiger’,‘Lion’

A DataLoaders includes validation and training DataLoader. Let’s check random validation dataset.

dls.valid.show_batch(max_n=6, nrows=2)

Squishing or Padding for Model Training :

  • Squishing or padding is applied to images during training.
  • Cropping may result in data loss, while squishing/stretching can lead to unrealistic shapes, impacting accuracy.
  • Padding may introduce excessive empty space, causing wasted computation.

Practical Approach - Data Augmentation: The idea of getting different picture every time from same image is called data augmentation.

  • Randomly select and crop parts of the image during each epoch.
  • Train the model on different image parts across multiple epochs.
  • This approach creates random variations in input data without altering its meaning.
  • Aiming to provide diverse perspectives, it ensures that the model sees different pictures from the same image in each iteration..

To train our model, we’ll use RandomResizedCrop with an image size of 224 px, which is fairly standard for image classification, and default aug_transforms:

big_cat = big_cat.new(
    item_tfms=RandomResizedCrop(224, min_scale=0.5),
    batch_tfms=aug_transforms())
big_cat_dls = big_cat.dataloaders(path)
big_cat_dls.train.show_batch(max_n=8, nrows=2)
